lesson.title: The Germanic Core
lesson.subtitle: Hundreds of German words you already know without realizing it

hook.title: You Don't Start from Zero
hook.content:
You already know a little German: Hand means "hand," and Finger means "finger." Say them aloud.

Now try lernen — "to learn." Build it from lern + en, then use it in a sentence. The familiar words are your starting point; the history can wait.

footnotes.title: Proto-Germanic Roots
footnotes.content: Spoken roughly 500 BC to 500 AD across southern Scandinavia and northern Germany before expanding westward into the British Isles.

pattern.title: The Universal -en Infinitive
pattern.content: In English, we mark dictionary verbs with the preposition 'to' (to learn, to find, to sing). German does something cleaner: it attaches the suffix '-en' directly onto the end of the root. Strip '-en' and you find the English word staring right back at you.

footnotes.title: The Living English -en Suffix
footnotes.content: English still uses Germanic -en to turn words into verbs: bright → brighten, short → shorten, deep → deepen, wide → widen. German simply kept -en on all dictionary verbs!

pattern.linguist_note: Old English also possessed the infinitive suffix -an (e.g. singan, findan), which was gradually leveled to -en in Middle English and completely dropped during the Early Modern English period.

exercises.explanation: German attaches the universal infinitive suffix -en to Germanic verb roots.

What native English verb shares the exact root of 'singen'?
exercises.explanation: German 'singen' is the direct twin of English 'to sing'.

vocab_hints.note: cognate with archaic English 'mid' in 'midwife' (literally: with-woman)
English softened Germanic -ck- into -dge (Brücke ↔ bridge, Rücken ↔ ridge, Ecke ↔ edge)
same word as 'Dutch' in 'Pennsylvania Dutch' (German settlers in America who spoke Deutsch)

exercises.explanation: Verb in Position 2: 'Ich lerne...'. 'mit' means with (as in midwife), and 'Brücke' is bridge (cognate with ridge/Rücken).

summary.outcome: Recognize familiar German infinitives and use one in a simple sentence.
summary.takeaway: Whenever you see a German verb ending in -en, strip the ending to look for the English root.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next up: the Hidden Twins — Arm, Hand, Finger, Haus, Brot: the zero-shift words you already own, waiting to be recognized.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from The Germanic Core (I learn German with Brücke):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich lerne Deutsch mit Brücke" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of The Germanic Core without relying on short-term echo.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

bringen.etymology_derivation: Shared ancient Germanic mixed verb (bring/brought ↔ bringen/gebracht).

decke.etymology_derivation: Via decken 'to cover', Proto-Germanic *þakjaną — cognate with English deck, related to thatch. [wiktionary]

nächste.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Hamburg.
nächste.context_translation: Next week I am going to Hamburg.
nächste.etymology_derivation: The superlative of nah — the twin of next, which was originally nighest, the superlative of nigh. [wiktionary]

schmal.context_phrase: Der Weg ist schmal und steil.
schmal.context_translation: The path is narrow and steep.
schmal.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *smalaz 'narrow, small' — the page lists English small as the direct cognate; German kept the narrow sense. [wiktionary]

buche.context_phrase: Die Buche ist hoch und alt.
buche.context_translation: The beech is tall and old.
buche.etymology_derivation: From Old High German buohha, from Proto-West Germanic *bōku and *bōkijā. English beech is the listed cognate; the entry also notes a possible link to Buch, book. [wiktionary]

zeitschrift.context_phrase: Die Zeitschrift liegt auf dem Tisch.
zeitschrift.context_translation: The magazine is lying on the table.
zeitschrift.etymology_derivation: Zeit (time) + Schrift (writing, from schreiben — the scribe-root): writings of the time, a periodical. [wiktionary]

gesundheit.context_translation: Health is more important than money.
gesundheit.etymology_derivation: Gesund (healthy) plus -heit (-ness); the page documents gesund as cognate with English sound — the old healthy-word alive in English in of sound mind. [wiktionary]
